quote: So I propose that it makes sense to say that 1 and 0 are not in the probabilities
content: The essay's norm has a name among Bayesian statisticians: Cromwell's rule. Lindley coined it and endorsed it, after Cromwell's "I beseech you, in the bowels of Christ, think it possible you may be mistaken." Assign 0 or 1 only to logical truths and falsehoods, never to contingent claims about the world. The measure-zero cases Fable raises are points in continuous spaces, such as a particular infinite sequence or an exact real value. The propositions a reasoner actually holds are events of positive measure under any sensible density. On the die, Fable's own answer, "Enlarging the space to include it changes the model," is the essay's point. A belief about the world is a belief about which model is right, and the probability that "some face from 1 to 6" is the whole outcome space is below one. The tautology is 1 inside the model, and the essay is talking about the model.

quote: A famous proof called Cox’s Theorem (plus various extensions and refinements thereof) shows that all ways of representing uncertainties that obey some reasonable-sounding constraints, end up isomorphic to each other.
content: Cox's theorem places certainty and impossibility at the ends of the scale, and the essay's phrasing invites that objection. The essay's use of the theorem is narrower: representations satisfying the constraints are isomorphic, so odds and log odds are as legitimate as probabilities, and in the log-odds representation the endpoints sit at infinite evidence. Nothing in Cox's theorem says the endpoints can be reached by finite evidence, and conditionalization shows they cannot. Halpern's counterexample is real. The standard repair adds a density or refinement assumption over rich propositional domains (Paris 1994, The Uncertain Reasoner's Companion, book, no DOI), which is a mild condition for any agent reasoning about the world. The theorem supplies the scale, and the essay is making a point about which parts of the scale evidence can reach.

quote: just as negative and positive infinity, which do not obey the field axioms, are not in the real numbers
content: The field-axiom analogy is a poor one, since 0 and 1 are the field's identities, and that is conceded. The substantive point does not depend on it. Excluded values are those at which the operations break down, and 0 and 1 are where Bayesian updating breaks down: conditioning on a probability-0 event is undefined in the ratio definition, and a credence of 1 cannot be moved by any evidence. The log-odds point is not a feature of the coordinates either. It is a theorem about evidence: from any prior strictly between 0 and 1, finitely many observations with nonzero likelihoods leave the posterior strictly between 0 and 1. Log odds make that visible, since evidence adds, and reaching certainty from finite evidence would require an infinite sum. That fact is about what evidence can do.

quote: The main reason this would upset probability theorists is that we would need to rederive theorems previously obtained by assuming that we can marginalize over a joint probability by adding up all the pieces and having them sum to 1.
content: Nothing in the essay's proposal removes normalization within a model. What it removes is credence 1 in the model itself. The "magical symbol" for unconsidered possibilities is a catch-all hypothesis with non-zero prior, and the author of the regularity paper Fable cites is the person who made that respectable. Shimony's "tempered personalism" requires reserving a non-negligible prior for hypotheses not yet formulated, so that a surprising result can raise the catch-all and send the scientist looking (Shimony 1970, "Scientific Inference," in The Nature and Function of Scientific Theories, no DOI). Bayes' theorem runs unchanged on the enlarged partition. Popper functions handle conditioning on probability zero, as Fable says, and they are a tool the essay could use, not a refutation of it.

quote: Just as there are mathematicians who refuse to believe in the law of the excluded middle or infinite sets, I would like to be a probability theorist who doesn’t believe in absolute certainty.
content: Fable grants the essay's substantive claim: "an ideal agent should not assign 1 to any contingent empirical proposition, because such an assignment can never be revised by conditionalization." That is the claim. The title puts a norm in the form of a definition, which is rhetoric, and the essay admits it is an aspiration ("I would like to be a probability theorist who doesn't believe in absolute certainty"). On tautologies, the preceding essay addresses them. A human's credence that they have computed a tautology correctly is contingent, and logical induction now gives a formal framework in which bounded reasoners hold theorems below 1 until they have proved them (Garrabrant et al. 2016, arXiv:1609.03543). The system Fable asked for was built later, by the essay's own intellectual heirs.
